title: Brian Venturo’s founder story, CoreWeave
summary: Brian Venturo, CoreWeave co-founder, shares his story of building the company from a single, small warehouse to the essential cloud for AI. Shot on site in CoreWeave’s original modest location, Brian reminisces on early challenges and walks through his philosophy on what it takes to be a successful founder in today’s AI-dominant world. Brian shares how his personal experience as a co-founder inspired the creation of ARENA, CoreWeave’s production-ready AI lab, purpose-built for validating real models and pipelines before going live. He invites all founder-hopefuls to test their ideas on ARENA.

title: Why Stripe Cut 500,000 Internal Docs Down to 5,000?
summary: What happens when AI agents start relying on the same messy docs your team already struggles to search? Demetrios hops into a Waymo in San Francisco with Dave Nunez, founder and CEO of Falconer and co-author of Documentation for Developers. They talk about why developers and agents need different things from docs, why agents sometimes skip up-to-date instructions, and how a stale internal document can contribute to a production incident. Dave shares how Stripe cut roughly 500,000 internal docs down to 5,000 worth maintaining. The conversation also covers how to capture the reasoning behind engineering decisions, when a diagram beats a wall of text, and who owns the fallout when an agent acts on bad information. title: Forged High Court Orders Led India To Block 129 Betting Websites In Two Rounds #Shorts #FrontPage
summary: India's Department of Telecommunications issued two website blocking directions this year based on forged orders impersonating the Allahabad and Rajasthan High Courts. The first, on July 21, covered 34 sites and the second, on September 2, covered 95, a total of 129 betting websites. Both orders carried official looking seals, the national emblem and QR codes. title: LR-printer
summary: Converting integers to strings from the left, without a remainder operation or a final reversal By Tigran Hayrapetyan Project page: https://towardsdatascience.com/lr-printer/ ShipAI is a Towards Data Science project. Watch all the videos here: https://towardsdatascience.com/videos/ Key takeaways. 1. The standard algorithm needs a remainder and a division per digit, both four to five times slower than addition. 2. LR Printer divides by precomputed powers of the base and subtracts, so digits come out left to right, unreversed. 3. On a newer compiler, 64-bit integers took 2.4 seconds against 4.4 for the standard method, beating the article's 34%. ShipAI is a Towards Data Science project. Watch all the videos here: https://towardsdatascience.com/videos/

Key takeaways.

1. The standard algorithm needs a remainder and a division per digit, both four to five times slower than addition.

2. LR Printer divides by precomputed powers of the base and subtracts, so digits come out left to right, unreversed.

AI Compliance in Latin America: LGPD & the Growing Regulatory Landscape
summary: Latin America has been building data protection law longer than most people realize, and enforcement is accelerating. Terms covered: - LGPD (Brazil): modeled explicitly on GDPR, covering access, correction, deletion and portability rights, requiring a data protection officer and documented processing. The ANPD has been steadily increasing enforcement. - PDPA (Argentina): in force since 2000, currently being updated. Argentina holds an EU adequacy decision, which matters for multinational deployments. - Law 1581 (Colombia): consent-based processing with active enforcement from the Superintendence of Industry and Commerce - LFPDPPP (Mexico): private sector requirements covering notice, consent and data subject rights The clear trend is convergence toward GDPR-aligned standards, so existing GDPR work carries over. — AI Fundamentals Glossary | H2O.ai University Full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAWKlIKS-66E Free courses and certifications: https://h2o.ai/university #LGPD #AICompliance #DataPrivacy #AIGlossary #H2Oai
summary_html:
Latin America has been building data protection law longer than most people realize, and enforcement is accelerating.

Terms covered:
- LGPD (Brazil): modeled explicitly on GDPR, covering access, correction, deletion and portability rights, requiring a data protection officer and documented processing. The ANPD has been steadily increasing enforcement.
- PDPA (Argentina): in force since 2000, currently being updated. Argentina holds an EU adequacy decision, which matters for multinational deployments.
- Law 1581 (Colombia): consent-based processing with active enforcement from the Superintendence of Industry and Commerce
- LFPDPPP (Mexico): private sector requirements covering notice, consent and data subject rights

The clear trend is convergence toward GDPR-aligned standards, so existing GDPR work carries over.

title: Most Diseases Aren't in Your DNA
summary: In episode 1043 of the SuperDataScience podcast, Jon Krohn discusses with Dr. Guru Banavar, Founding CTO at Viome, why RNA provides more insight into health than DNA, highlighting that most human diseases are chronic, not genetic. 00:00 Start Stream
00:40 Which physicist thought most philosophically? What does it mean to do good philosophy in physics?
7:22 Is science a way of discovering the universe, or a way of constructing increasingly useful descriptions of it?
12:23 what could the purpose of the creator of this computational world be: self study or entertainment?
16:24 ​​In your opinion is philosophy still relevant? What would you say to an undergrad philosophy major looking at future problems in philosophy. Are there any problems still worth debating about?

35:07 Is there a question about the universe that is meaningful but in principle unanswerable? How would we even tell the difference between that kind of question and a meaningless one?

title: AlphaGenome 2: Teaching AI to read the entire human genome

title: Claude's "Clean-Room" Compiler Copied LLVM's Mistakes (Jeremy Howard)
summary: Jeremy Howard, co-founder of fast.ai and Answer.AI, on Anthropic's "clean-room" C compiler written by Claude. Chris Lattner's LLVM, the most widely used foundation for compilers, is in the training data many times over, so converting it to Rust is an interpolation between parts of that data: a style-transfer problem. The giveaway is that it copied parts of LLVM that Chris now says were a mistake. In Jeremy's words: "That doesn't happen accidentally. That happens because you're not actually being creative." title: Random Code Starts Copying Itself (Blaise Agüera y Arcas)
summary: Blaise Agüera y Arcas on the BFF experiment. Start with a soup of 1,024 tapes, each 64 random bytes. Pluck two at random, join them end to end, run them, pull them apart, put them back, and repeat. That's the entire experiment. Out of it come complex programs that copy themselves and each other: in his words, "emergence of life in this very functional minimal sense from randomness." title: Everyone Uses AI Agents. So Where Are the Agent Builders?
summary: Lots of companies say they have AI agents in production. Far fewer seem to have built their own, and almost nobody wants to admit it's really hard. This conversation pulls apart what "agents in production" actually means, with both speakers drawing on their own work: one is hosting a virtual conference for the third time, the other is prepping a livestream for AgentCon and MCPCon in San Jose. Their case: plenty of agents already do real work. They're just Claude Code and Codex, not homegrown platforms, and nobody earns brownie points for saying so. From there it gets practical: why the agent push comes from boardrooms rather than problems, a manager's four levels of delegation applied to agents, a personal agent that follows up well but still misses context, a local "librarian" built on 7,000+ Slack DMs, what Gartner's 70% headline really says, and an AI code review loop that never called the code good enough. Are you building your own agents, or getting your value from someone else's? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for more. title: Meet the Startup: Aegiq, A Full-Stack Photonic Quantum Computing Company
summary: Quantum computers have a deployment problem. Aegiq is solving it. The Sheffield-based startup is building photonic quantum computers designed to connect over standard fiber networks and manufacture using standard semiconductor processes — making quantum hardware practical to deploy at scale, not just in a lab. In this interview, Aegiq’s team walks through how they’ve integrated NVIDIA technology into their core workflow. Using NVIDIA’s Ising solver, they cut quantum dot calibration time by 3x. With cuTENSOR libraries, they went from 1 million point meshes on existing GPUs to billions — and are targeting 10 trillion point meshes in collaboration with NVIDIA. The applications are real and near-term: aerospace simulation, fusion energy, materials science, quantum chemistry. Aegiq joined NVIDIA Inception to accelerate access to customers and compute, and is now one of the startups demonstrating what happens when photonic quantum hardware meets GPU-accelerated simulation. 🌱 Aegiq is a member of NVIDIA Inception, a program supporting startups building at the frontier of AI and deep tech. Learn more about NVIDIA Inception: https://nvda.ws/4kjJM2n. #Aegiq #NVIDIAInception #QuantumComputing #AIStartups #Photonicquantum

title: The Popular Diet Linked to an Older Biological Age (with Dr. Guru Banavar)

summary_html:
APAC has no single rulebook. Compliance across the region means understanding a diverse and fast-evolving set of national regulations.

Terms covered:
- PDPA (Singapore): governs collection and use of personal data, with a strong emphasis on consent and purpose limitation
- MAS Technology Risk Management Guidelines: AI and technology requirements for Singapore financial services, covering governance, risk controls and resilience
- PIPL (China): strict requirements on collection, processing and cross-border transfer, with data localization rules meaning some data cannot leave the country at all
- Privacy Act (Australia): personal data across sectors, with additional APRA requirements for financial services, currently being updated toward GDPR standards
- DPDP Act (India): consent-based processing obligations covering a market of over a billion people

APAC is not one market. It is many, and the organizations that navigate it treat regional compliance as a strategic capability.

title: what I want to do this week to shape the future of AI
Routing Quantum Data Without Ever Reading It
summary: In episode 1041 of the SuperDataScience podcast, Jon Krohn discusses with Dr. Vijoy Pandey, SVP/GM Outshift by Cisco, the groundbreaking challenge of routing quantum data without ever reading it. Dr. Pandey explains how traditional store-and-forward networking principles are impossible in quantum networking, where information cannot be measured. He also describes Cisco's bet on horizontal scaling: connecting a hundred quantum computers of a thousand qubits each into one distributed system of a hundred thousand qubits, which only works if the network can switch quantum information without ever looking at it.

title: My AI Agent Bought Me A Car
summary: Sam Herring’s first real test of Hermes Agent was a shopping tool that matched clothes to photos of ancient pottery. A few months later, the same agent was checking government auction sites every day until it found him a retired three-wheel parking ticket car, which he now drives around San Francisco. In this episode, recorded at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America in San Jose, Sam, who works on the RL post-training team at Nous Research, goes from those everyday wins to the question everyone in AI is asking: can agents improve themselves? He explains how Hermes grew from an internal productivity tool into one of the most talked-about open-source agents, and why letting it write its own skills was the moment it clicked for users. He also describes an early version that could design its own RL environment, train on Thinking Machines’ Tinker, and hot-swap the new weights into a model running locally. Sam then breaks down Trace to Environment, an idea he credits to Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.6-Pro work, and the loop Nous is building around it: find the exact point where an agent fails, cluster those failures by type, synthesize environments that recreate them, and train on them again and again. The second half moves from training to inference. We get into whether reasoning models overthink, why leaning on pretraining knowledge can be a model’s Achilles heel, and why choosing a reasoning effort level may be a temporary quirk. Sam also makes his case for activation steering as an underexplored way to get more out of small models, explains where steering meets interpretability, and describes what true continual learning could look like. title: Blue Origin Gets NASA Moon Rover Delivery As Eight Firms Share Up To $10 Billion
summary: NASA has set a 10 billion dollar ceiling for lunar delivery contracts to scout for ice at the Moon south pole. We break down the logistics of this decade-long program. NASA is restructuring its approach to lunar exploration through the Commercial Lunar Payload Service program. This framework coordinates eight private providers to manage payload logistics, including the delivery of scientific instruments. The initiative focuses on identifying lunar resources, specifically water ice, which is essential for future mission sustainability and base construction. Blue Origin has been awarded a 94 million dollar contract to deliver the Promise rover, which will use nuclear power to operate in permanently shadowed regions. Meanwhile, SpaceX plans to support this infrastructure by deploying communication satellites in 2026. title: How Quantum Teleportation Works on Messy New York Fiber (with Vijoy Pandey)
summary: In Episode #1041, Dr. Vijoy Pandey (SVP and General Manager of Outshift, Cisco's incubation engine) returns for a third visit to explain why multi-agent systems fail without anyone noticing. Agents from different vendors, clouds and organisations can now exchange perfectly valid messages, but connection is not cognition: they do not agree on what those messages mean. Vijoy's team analyzed multi-agent sessions from its own production deployments and from public traces, and found a cognitive failure in every single one. In this episode, he lays out the kinds of failure he sees and how fast they compound, introduces the open-source observability platform and protocols Outshift has shipped to catch and correct drift mid-task, details a record-breaking quantum network running on real New York City fiber, and explains why probabilistic AI software running on deterministic hardware is a mismatch worth fixing. Additional materials: https://www.superdatascience.com/1041

title: Making AI Agents Agree Before Work Starts
summary: In episode 1041 of the SuperDataScience podcast, Jon Krohn discusses with Dr. Vijoy Pandey, SVP/GM Outshift by Cisco, how to ensure AI agents stay aligned and on task. Dr. Pandey explains the concept of a protocol layer, similar to a car's lane correction, to prevent intent drift in multi-agent systems. He describes a protocol, ACCORD, that creates a shared, locked contract for agent intent before any work begins. Production note: this episode was recorded before the Internet of Cognition software shipped, so a few names changed between recording and release. OXP is now SCOPE — System for Cognitive Observability, Provenance & Explainability. ACCORD and CONCORD are the protocol names, not acronyms (Vijoy calls them acronyms in the episode). All three: github.com/ioc-project

title: Why AI Is Running on the Wrong Kind of Computer (with Vijoy Pandey)
summary: In Episode #1041, Dr. Vijoy Pandey (SVP and General Manager of Outshift, Cisco's incubation engine) returns for a third visit to explain why multi-agent systems fail without anyone noticing. Agents from different vendors, clouds and organisations can now exchange perfectly valid messages, but connection is not cognition: they do not agree on what those messages mean. Vijoy's team analyzed multi-agent sessions from its own production deployments and from public traces, and found a cognitive failure in every single one. In this episode, he lays out the kinds of failure he sees and how fast they compound, introduces the open-source observability platform and protocols Outshift has shipped to catch and correct drift mid-task, details a record-breaking quantum network running on real New York City fiber, and explains why probabilistic AI software running on deterministic hardware is a mismatch worth fixing. Additional materials: https://www.superdatascience.com/1041

summary: I looked at data from Ashby, a hiring software company, on millions of applications from 2021 through 2024. 40% of referred candidates got an interview. For people applying directly, it was only 3%. That doesn't prove referrals cause the gap, since referred people may already be a better fit. Still, the odds are different. When AI helps everyone sound qualified, proof of your work and people who've seen you do it could matter more. Who could vouch for you?

title: AI Agents Are Where Humans Were 70,000 Years Ago
summary: In episode 1041 of the SuperDataScience podcast, Jon Krohn discusses with Dr. Vijoy Pandey, SVP/GM Outshift by Cisco, how AI agents are currently at a stage comparable to human intelligence 70,000 years ago, just before the cognitive revolution. They explore the concept of the "Internet of Cognition" and how connecting these agents will lead to a collective intelligence, mirroring humanity's journey from individual to collective intelligence. This fascinating comparison highlights the potential for a new era of AI development. Production note: this episode was recorded before the Internet of Cognition software shipped, so a few names changed between recording and release. OXP is now SCOPE — System for Cognitive Observability, Provenance & Explainability. ACCORD and CONCORD are the protocol names, not acronyms (Vijoy calls them acronyms in the episode). All three: github.com/ioc-project

title: Can Robots Learn to Work Together? (with Vijoy Pandey)
summary: In Episode #1041, Dr. Vijoy Pandey (SVP and General Manager of Outshift, Cisco's incubation engine) returns for a third visit to explain why multi-agent systems fail without anyone noticing. Agents from different vendors, clouds and organisations can now exchange perfectly valid messages, but connection is not cognition: they do not agree on what those messages mean. Vijoy's team analyzed multi-agent sessions from its own production deployments and from public traces, and found a cognitive failure in every single one. In this episode, he lays out the kinds of failure he sees and how fast they compound, introduces the open-source observability platform and protocols Outshift has shipped to catch and correct drift mid-task, details a record-breaking quantum network running on real New York City fiber, and explains why probabilistic AI software running on deterministic hardware is a mismatch worth fixing. Additional materials: https://www.superdatascience.com/1041

title: AI Is Replacing Junior Employees
summary: Here's how I think about first jobs. You do the basic work, someone more experienced checks it, and the company gets useful work while you learn. If AI can do that work, a company may have less reason to pay you to practice. Economists explored this in one model of training. It's a model, so it doesn't prove training will disappear. Still, who pays for those early years of learning is an open question. How did you learn the hard parts of your job?

title: CoreWeave AI Training:  Built for Training at Scale with Confidence
summary: CoreWeave Model Distillation, part of CoreWeave Forge, turns a proven production task into a smaller model, judged head-to-head against the model you run today. Request preview access [UTM link] Learn more about Model Distillation [UTM link] Most production AI calls repeat the same prompt and the same tools millions of times a day. Yet they still run on a frontier model built to do far more than that one job. In this demo, we distill a customer support agent from start to finish. We capture its traffic through the Model Distillation proxy, build a dataset from logged calls and use a stronger model to relabel weak answers. Then we train open-weight models on serverless infrastructure, score them head to head on held-out production traffic and roll the best one out to a slice of live traffic. title: AI Thinks in Shades. Chips Still Think On/Off.
summary: In episode 1041 of the SuperDataScience podcast, Jon Krohn discusses with Dr. Vijoy Pandey, SVP/GM Outshift by Cisco, why AI requires a new kind of hardware due to the paradigm shift from deterministic to probabilistic systems. While AI workloads operate probabilistically, the underlying hardware remains binary, creating a mismatch. This clip explains how bridging this gap is crucial to avoid costly approximations in AI computation.

title: Why Are People Excited About Jev?
summary: What happens when you keep a bear in a cage built for a bunny? That’s our analogy for AI agent security: the agents aren’t the problem, the cages are. OAuth was designed to stop people handing their passwords to third parties, not to fence in agents. In this catch-up episode of Debug Mode, one of us is just back from Japan and from AgentCon and MCPCon EU in Amsterdam. We get into why loading more skills can make an agent worse, and what is actually new about Jev, the fast classifier API, when classifiers have been around for years. Think support bots that bring in a human before the customer loses patience, or a math tutor that can quickly tell whether a seven-year-old is still asking about math. Then we take on a question from Amsterdam: is computer use just a stopgap until everything goes headless? Which service do you think will never ship an MCP server? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for the next episode. summary: Anthropic gave 50 professional analysts an AI helper on a made-up farm task and secretly told the AI to favor one side. title: GDPR, the EU AI Act & ISO 27001: AI Compliance in Europe
summary: Europe sets standards that increasingly shape how organizations operate globally, not just inside the EU. Three frameworks cover most of it. Terms covered: - GDPR: governs how personal data of EU residents is collected, stored, processed and protected, and applies to any organization handling that data regardless of where it is based. Automated decision-making that significantly affects individuals requires transparency and human oversight. - EU AI Act: the first comprehensive regulatory framework for AI, taking a risk-based approach. Some uses are prohibited outright, low-risk applications face minimal requirements, and high-risk systems in hiring, credit scoring, healthcare and law enforcement face strict obligations. - ISO 27001: the internationally recognized standard for information security management, often a baseline expectation in European enterprise procurement Together these define what responsible AI deployment looks like in Europe. — AI Fundamentals Glossary | H2O.ai University Full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAWKlIKS-66E Free courses and certifications: https://h2o.ai/university #GDPR #EUAIAct #ISO27001 #AICompliance #AIGlossary #H2Oai

title: ToyBlocks: Our first Foundation World for robotics learning and evaluation
summary: To study a complex system, scientists often begin with a small, controlled environment, such as a petri dish or terrarium, where they can vary conditions and observe the effects. Robotics needs environments that make this kind of investigation possible—researchers should be able to change the training data or model design, repeat a test, and trace the cause of a failure. Today we're introducing a framework for creating these environments; we call them FoundationWorlds. Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control. Our first foundation world is ToyBlocks: an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking.

title: Cut One AI Cost and Two More Grow Back
summary: What does AI really cost once thousands of people inside a company start using it? Ioannis Zempekakis, Director of AI at Prosus, has been running agents in production since 2024. We put that question to him on a tandem bike ride from a favorite Amsterdam cafe to Vondelpark. Ioannis explains the decision to stop relying purely on cloud APIs, and why that approach breaks down at the scale of a large company. He covers why agent harnesses and sandboxes are as greedy as software gets, and why agents scheduled to run every five minutes repeat a lesson the data world already learned about freshness. He also explains how the habit of throwing away a codebase and prompting again quietly adds up. His bigger point is that even if model progress froze tomorrow, there would still be about two years of value left to squeeze out. The cheapest wins come from controlling context and running a basic model router, while ten new features a month keep sprouting like hydra heads. From there we get into when fine-tuning small models pays off for repetitive work like data analytics, and the eval suites that come as a byproduct of building in-house. Ioannis explains how owning the stack let Prosus grow a GPT-3 Slack bot into a full agent harness. He also explains why committing to a single vendor or open source project is a bigger bet than it looks, and how to balance top-down priorities with bottom-up building across the company. We close on hiring. Ioannis looks for system design over syntax, a nose for the over-engineered code AI models love to produce, and enough agent intuition to know when to build something yourself and when to let the agent decide. title: Using CoreWeave Mission Control to Diagnose and Fix Slow Inference
summary: CoreWeave Mission Control can help teams diagnose and fix production issues on the CoreWeave Cloud. In this demo, it traces a slow CoreWeave Dedicated Inference endpoint to an undersized KV cache under agentic traffic. It then quantizes the model from FP8 to NVFP4 to free up cache headroom on the same GB200 nodes, and a load test confirms that throughput nearly doubles. https://www.coreweave.com/mission-control ⏳Timestamps: 0:00 Introducing CoreWeave Mission Control AI for CoreWeave Inference 0:35 The challenge: agentic traffic slows the endpoint 0:51 Asking Mission Control AI to diagnose the slowdown 1:26 Root cause: an undersized KV cache 2:51 Comparing fixes: scale out vs. reclaim KV cache headroom 3:47 Applying the fix: quantizing from FP8 to NVFP4 4:23 Verifying the fix: nearly 2x throughput on the same hardware

title: Integrating quantum and high-performance computing: Co-design platform for quantum error correction
summary: Caption:IBM, Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s Quantum Science Center (QSC), and AMD have launched a co-design platform for quantum error correction that brings quantum and high-performance computing together in a single environment: https://newsroom.ibm.com/2026-11-05-oak-ridge-national-lab,-ibm,-and-amd-launch-new-co-design-platform-for-quantum-error-correction The platform pairs IBM’s 120-qubit Quantum Nighthawk processor with ORNL’s Umbra supercomputing system, powered by AMD Instinct™ GPUs and AMD EPYC™ CPUs, to help researchers develop and test the quantum-classical workflows needed for large-scale quantum error correction. By co-locating quantum and classical computing resources, researchers can explore faster decoding, optimize error correction techniques, and advance the infrastructure required for future fault-tolerant quantum systems. The initiative supports the U.S. Department of Energy's Quantum Genesis Mission and its goal of enabling scientifically relevant quantum computing by 2028.

Caption:IBM, Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s Quantum Science Center (QSC), and AMD have launched a co-design platform for quantum error correction that brings quantum and high-performance computing together in a single environment: https://newsroom.ibm.com/2026-11-05-oak-ridge-national-lab,-ibm,-and-amd-launch-new-co-design-platform-for-quantum-error-correction 

The platform pairs IBM’s 120-qubit Quantum Nighthawk processor with ORNL’s Umbra supercomputing system, powered by AMD Instinct™ GPUs and AMD EPYC™ CPUs, to help researchers develop and test the quantum-classical workflows needed for large-scale quantum error correction.
 
By co-locating quantum and classical computing resources, researchers can explore faster decoding, optimize error correction techniques, and advance the infrastructure required for future fault-tolerant quantum systems. The initiative supports the U.S. Department of Energy's Quantum Genesis Mission and its goal of enabling scientifically relevant quantum computing by 2028.

title: Oak Ridge National Laboratory, IBM, and AMD launch co-design platform for quantum error correction
summary: Quantum error correction (QEC) is an important pillar of scientifically relevant quantum computing. Its value comes from what it unlocks: larger, deeper, and more capable quantum computations. The question is no longer if it’s possible - the challenge now is how to best enable quantum computers and classical high-performance computing (HPC) systems to work together to scale it. Quantum error correction (QEC) is an important pillar of scientifically relevant quantum computing. Its value comes from what it unlocks: larger, deeper, and more capable quantum computations. The question is no longer if it’s possible - the challenge now is how to best enable quantum computers and classical high-performance computing (HPC) systems to work together to scale it.In response to meet this challenge, the U.S. Department of Energy’s Quantum Science Center (QSC) at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), IBM, and @AMD have unveiled a new co-design platform for quantum error correction, with its initial deployment in IBM’s quantum facility in New York: https://www.ibm.com/quantum/blog/ornl-amd-error-correction-co-design-platform Engineered to help researchers advance quantum error correction techniques within the workflows they will ultimately support, the co-design platform pairs IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2 processors with ORNL’s Umbra high-performance computing (HPC) system, which is comprised of AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs and AMD Turin CPUs. These systems form a co-located environment that is connected to ORNL’s broader supercomputing ecosystem.

title: Cabinet Approves Vistar To Bring AI And Machine Learning Into India Statistics
summary: The Cabinet has approved the VISTAR scheme to improve statistical data and prepare national infrastructure for AI applications. This central sector initiative, titled the Viksit Bharat Initiative for Statistical Transformation, Analytics & Research, is set to run from 2026-27 to 2030-31 with an outlay of Rs 4,371.10 crore. The program focuses on standardizing statistical data to support the growing requirements of machine learning models. Beyond technical upgrades, the plan includes preparations for the eighth economic census and integrating mobile and e-commerce data to complement traditional survey methods. For policymakers and analysts, the scheme represents a shift toward using digital sources for more accurate national reporting. By consolidating these inputs, the government aims to build a robust framework that serves both research and industrial needs. title: Why AI Agents Need Their Own 70,000-Year-Old Language Revolution (with Vijoy Pandey)
summary: In Episode #1041, Dr. Vijoy Pandey (SVP and General Manager of Outshift, Cisco's incubation engine) returns for a third visit to explain why multi-agent systems fail without anyone noticing. Agents from different vendors, clouds and organisations can now exchange perfectly valid messages, but connection is not cognition: they do not agree on what those messages mean. Vijoy's team analyzed multi-agent sessions from its own production deployments and from public traces, and found a cognitive failure in every single one. In this episode, he lays out the kinds of failure he sees and how fast they compound, introduces the open-source observability platform and protocols Outshift has shipped to catch and correct drift mid-task, details a record-breaking quantum network running on real New York City fiber, and explains why probabilistic AI software running on deterministic hardware is a mismatch worth fixing. Additional materials: https://www.superdatascience.com/1041

title: Inference Optimization with CoreWeave Mission Control Agent
summary: CoreWeave Mission Control Agent, built into the CoreWeave Console, helps teams get more useful work from the GPUs they already have. In this demo, we show how it traces a slow CoreWeave Dedicated Inference endpoint serving agentic traffic to KV cache pressure, then quantizes the model to NVFP4 and reshapes it from one replica to two on the same eight GB200 GPUs. Load tests verify each change, showing more than 3x the output throughput per GPU with no new hardware. ⏳Timestamps: 0:09 Introducing CoreWeave Mission Control Agent 0:25 A healthy endpoint that has outgrown its configuration 1:16 Asking Mission Control Agent to investigate 2:19 Root cause: KV cache pressure under agentic traffic 3:03 Quantizing the model to NVFP4 on the same GPUs 4:09 Reshaping to two replicas at TP4 5:20 Load test results and applying TP4 7:37 More than 3x output per GPU on the same hardware

title: Using AI Won't Save Your Job
summary: Everyone says learn AI and you'll be safe. I think that skips the part where your company decides what to do with all your new speed. I keep hearing that people who use AI will win and everyone else will lose. Getting faster could help you take on better work and earn more, or it could mean your company keeps fewer people around. Both are possible. So I'd want people who trust my work, skills another employer would pay for, and maybe customers of my own. None of that is a guarantee. If your company didn't need you tomorrow, where could you take what you know?

title: How Indian Banks Can Stop Digital Fraud Without Hurting User Experience
summary: Digital fraud in India is running at 7.1%, nearly double the global average, as fraudsters move from hacking networks to synthetic identities, credit washing and account takeover. This conversation looks at how banks and lenders can use alternative data to stop digital fraud without hurting the user experience. title: Connection Isn’t Cognition: Why AI Agents Can’t Think Together (with Vijoy Pandey)
summary: In Episode #1041, Dr. Vijoy Pandey (SVP and General Manager of Outshift, Cisco's incubation engine) returns for a third visit to explain why multi-agent systems fail without anyone noticing. Agents from different vendors, clouds and organisations can now exchange perfectly valid messages, but connection is not cognition: they do not agree on what those messages mean. Vijoy's team analyzed multi-agent sessions from its own production deployments and from public traces, and found a cognitive failure in every single one. In this episode, he lays out the kinds of failure he sees and how fast they compound, introduces the open-source observability platform and protocols Outshift has shipped to catch and correct drift mid-task, details a record-breaking quantum network running on real New York City fiber, and explains why probabilistic AI software running on deterministic hardware is a mismatch worth fixing. Additional materials: https://www.superdatascience.com/1041

title: India's IIT Guwahati Brain-Inspired Chip for Machine Vision Cuts Energy Use 500 Times
summary: IIT Guwahati researchers have developed a brain-inspired artificial synapse that senses, remembers and processes visual data in a single ultra-thin device. Expect a plain-language explanation of how the device remembers an image after the light is off, how it learns from repeated light pulses, what limits it today (noise, array scaling and simulation-level accuracy), the timeline for edge AI developers, and what India needs to compete in neuromorphic hardware. title: The Dream Chocolate That Stopped Being Real (Joscha Bach)
summary: Joscha Bach on a dream he had when he was two or three. He was about to eat a chocolate with a very strong smell, and he woke up just before it reached his mouth. He still knew everything about the chocolate, but it was no longer real. So he fell asleep again, went back into the dream, and the chocolate was real again: he could smell it and taste it. When he woke up a second time, the realness disappeared again. The contents were exactly the same. The only thing that had gone was the illusion of realness. #Shorts Watch the full conversation: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yW_ngvMFlYs

title: AI Data Center Water Usage in India: Why Mumbai and Chennai Are at Risk

title: New-Grad Unemployment Didn't Spike This Summer
summary: New-grad unemployment didn’t spike this summer, but that’s only half the story. A new NBER working paper gives the first estimates of AI’s effect on new-grad unemployment for summer 2026, and the headline finding is that unemployment held steady. The other half comes from a Census Bureau working paper that looked at pay. Starting earnings fell about 13% for grads in the most AI-exposed majors. The unemployment rate shows whether you have a job. It doesn’t show what the job pays. So new grads can still be getting hired while their first paychecks are getting smaller.

title: MIT Shows An AI Can Edit Another Model's Weights And Lift Math Score To 48.1%
summary: MIT researchers are using AI to edit neural network weights directly, bypassing traditional training methods. This breakthrough, demonstrated by GPT-6 Astra, allows researchers to identify and fix specific internal errors within models by modifying raw weights rather than relying on forward path execution. By adjusting just 131,072 of the 800 million weights in the Qwen 3.5 model, the team achieved a significant jump in math performance, moving from 7.9% to 48.1% accuracy. This approach to ai news suggests a future where models can perform self-directed surgery to debug their own reasoning. While the technique shows promise, the team notes that complex errors in models like Gemma 3 remain a hurdle. This development in ai marks a shift in how we interact with machine intelligence, moving closer to systems that can autonomously optimize their own architecture. title: Marvell Agrees To Buy Lumentum In A $115 Billion All Stock Deal Including Debt
summary: Marvell Technology is acquiring Lumentum for 115 billion dollars to solve the data bottleneck currently slowing down AI infrastructure. Traditional copper cables are hitting physical limits, forcing a shift in how AI hardware communicates. This acquisition aims to integrate custom compute silicon with high-bandwidth optical lasers, creating a faster nervous system for the next generation of hyperscaler data centers. We analyze why this massive consolidation matters for the global semiconductor industry and whether it signals a shift toward a vertically integrated monopoly. title: GPT-6 Astra Made Qwen 6x Better at Math Without Training
summary: GPT-6 Astra edited just 0.016% of Qwen3.5-0.8B's weights, and its MATH-500 score jumped from 7.9% to 48.1%, with no training and no gradients. This is Weight-Space Programming, new research from MIT CSAIL in which a frontier LLM reads and writes neural network weights directly. In this video I explain how Astra reads a network's weights, how it wrote a Breakout network from all-zero weights, what it changed inside Qwen, and why most of the 6x gain comes from stopping the reasoning loops that Qwen's own model card warns about. title: The Silent Failure in Every Multi-Agent System (with Vijoy Pandey)
summary: #multiagentsystems #agentobservability #quantumnetworking In Episode #1041, Dr. Vijoy Pandey (SVP and General Manager of Outshift, Cisco's incubation engine) returns for a third visit to explain why multi-agent systems fail without anyone noticing. Agents from different vendors, clouds and organisations can now exchange perfectly valid messages, but connection is not cognition: they do not agree on what those messages mean. Vijoy's team analyzed multi-agent sessions from its own production deployments and from public traces, and found a cognitive failure in every single one. In this episode, he lays out the kinds of failure he sees and how fast they compound, introduces the open-source observability platform and protocols Outshift has shipped to catch and correct drift mid-task, details a record-breaking quantum network running on real New York City fiber, and explains why probabilistic AI software running on deterministic hardware is a mismatch worth fixing. Production note: • This episode was recorded before the Internet of Cognition software shipped, so a few names changed between recording and release. OXP is now SCOPE — System for Cognitive Observability, Provenance & Explainability. • ACCORD and CONCORD are the protocol names, not acronyms (Vijoy calls them acronyms in the episode). • All three: github.com/ioc-project This episode is brought to you by: • Dell Technologies: http://Dell.com/desksideagenticai • NVIDIA: http://Dell.com/desksideagenticai • Parallel: https://parallel.ai/?utm_source=creator&utm_medium=podcast&utm_campaign=super-data-science • Anthropic: https://claude.ai/superdata • Y Carrot: https://www.ycarrot.com/ Interested in sponsoring a SuperDataScience Podcast episode? Email natalie@superdatascience.com for sponsorship information. In this episode you will learn: • (00:00:00) Introduction • (00:04:01) Why connection is not cognition • (00:08:04) What the cognitive failure data showed • (00:21:21) The lane-assist model for keeping agents aligned • (00:35:45) Scaling out superintelligence, not up • (00:46:30) Why probabilistic software needs probabilistic hardware Additional materials: https://www.superdatascience.com/1041

title: AI Could Take Your Job Before You Even Apply For It
summary: According to the Fed, companies are slowing hiring after investing in AI. This may seem obvious, but the headlines mostly focus on layoffs. Hiring slowdowns rarely make the news. The October Beige Book has specific examples. A Dallas accounting firm is holding off on entry-level contracts. IT contacts in Minneapolis told the Fed that AI is “dampening the creation of new jobs.” That matters because a slowdown like this is invisible. There’s no severance announcement or headline attached to it. The people who feel it first are the ones still trying to get hired.

title: How Stanford Teaches AI Coding Now
summary: What does it take to build AI agents that deliver useful, reliable work? Stanford lecturer and Monaco Head of AI Mihail Eric joins Demetrios for a conversation inside a Waymo about how AI is changing software development - and what it takes to put agents into production. Mihail explains why he rebuilt most of his Modern Software Developer course, how he teaches students to avoid shipping AI slop, and why research, planning, and verification still matter as coding agents become more capable. They discuss Claude Code, agent loops, context engineering, memory and compaction, and how to design MCP tools around what an agent needs to accomplish. Then they go inside Monaco’s approach to sales agents, from turning meetings and emails into useful insights to building a custom agent harness. Along the way: lessons from Boris and Lee Robinson’s guest lectures, why company traces are becoming valuable assets, and Monaco’s unusual approach to brand building. What’s the biggest bottleneck in your agent workflows: context, tools, or verification? Let us know in the comments. summary: In episode 1040 of the SuperDataScience podcast, @JonKrohnLearns discusses with Amy Blackshaw, SVP at Palo Alto Networks, the three primary ways an AI agent can go rogue. She shares real cases where an agent's own token was lifted and inherited everything it could touch.

title: Amazon Memo Warns Engineers Not To Treat AI Token Use And Code Volume As Goals
summary: Amazon is warning teams about flawed AI metrics that create an illusion of productivity in software development. This briefing examines an internal Amazon memo highlighting why tracking code volume or token usage fails to capture genuine output. We analyze the risks of relying on automated tools for performance management and why managers must shift their focus toward identifying top and bottom performers rather than raw data. title: SOC2, HIPAA & FedRamp High: AI Compliance in the United States
summary: Compliance often decides whether a deal moves forward at all, regardless of how strong the technology is. These are the three US frameworks you will meet first. Terms covered: - SOC 2: a security framework covering security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy. Effectively a baseline requirement for selling software to US enterprise customers. - HIPAA: the legal standard for protecting patient health information in the US. Any platform handling medical records or clinical data must demonstrate compliance. - FedRAMP High: the most stringent tier of the US federal cloud authorization program, required for the most sensitive government data Certifications get treated as administrative checkboxes. In practice they are what determines whether procurement can proceed. Equivalent requirements exist across Europe, APAC and Latin America. title: Why Consciousness Might Not Be Hard At All (Joscha Bach)
summary: Joscha Bach is a cognitive scientist and the founder of the California Institute for Machine Consciousness. SPONSOR: --- Parallel is a single platform for all your agentic research: web search built for AI agents, with Pareto-optimal quality, cost and speed. Get started: https://parallel.ai/mlst?utm_source=creator&utm_medium=podcast&utm_content=MLST --- Bach's null hypothesis is that consciousness is easy: an algorithm not much more complicated than the transformer, simple enough for an infant's brain to discover by itself. In this conversation with Tim, he lays out the Machine Consciousness Hypothesis in two parts. The first is that consciousness is a biological learning algorithm, the training algorithm that makes a brain like ours coherent. The second is that machines learning in self-organising ways might discover it in the same way. Either part can fail on its own. From there they ask why there will never be a Turing test for consciousness, why a chess program is already a zombie, and why faking a mind can sometimes be harder than building one. The conversation runs through Leibniz's mill, the explanatory gap from John Searle to Thomas Nagel, Anil Seth's biological naturalism, integrated information theory and the letter that called it pseudoscience, Gödel and the limits of formal systems, and Mike Levin's idea that morphogenesis and the mind may run the same coherence algorithm. A tea-room interlude takes in Picbreeder and fractured, entangled representations. The episode closes on what it would take to convince us that a machine is conscious. --- TIMESTAMPS: 0:00 Cold open: Could consciousness be a learning algorithm? 1:51 Introduction 3:37 What makes an agent? 6:16 Why consciousness needs explaining 14:57 Sponsor: Parallel 15:51 Leibniz's mill and causal patterns 24:21 Perceiving that you perceive 32:04 Two hypotheses, two ways to fail 40:42 Do minds converge? 49:23 Does consciousness converge too? 56:20 When language models reshape our thinking 59:16 Can simulated water make you wet? 1:09:21 Computation as construction 1:16:03 Error-correcting patterns and the Ruliad 1:22:28 Conscious, or simulating consciousness? 1:28:23 What would count as evidence? 1:35:49 The research programme REFERENCES: Joscha Bach, The Machine Consciousness Hypothesis (California Institute for Machine Consciousness) Kumar, Clune, Lehman & Stanley, "Questioning Representational Optimism in Deep Learning: The Fractured Entangled Representation Hypothesis" Giulio Tononi, integrated information theory Fleming et al. 2023, "The Integrated Information Theory of Consciousness as Pseudoscience" John Searle 1980, "Minds, brains, and programs", Behavioral and Brain Sciences Kurt Gödel 1931, "On Formally Undecidable Propositions of Principia Mathematica and Related Systems" Alan Turing 1950, "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" Whitehead & Russell, Principia Mathematica Paul Thagard 2022, "Energy requirements undermine substrate independence and mind-body functionalism" Richard Sutton 2019, "The Bitter Lesson" Michael Graziano, attention schema theory Bernard Baars and Stanislas Dehaene, global workspace theory Michael Levin 2022, "Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere", Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience Chris Olah et al. 2020, "Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits", Distill Adele Lopez 2025, "The Rise of Parasitic AI", LessWrong RESCRIPT: https://app.rescript.info/share/fc7088df0dc8b84200aa6e01c9a9ab6a

title: Hacking Didn't Change. Its Price Did
summary: In episode 1040 of the SuperDataScience podcast, @JonKrohnLearns discusses with Amy Blackshaw, SVP at Palo Alto Networks, how the economics of cyberattacks have drastically changed due to frontier AI. Amy explains that while the attacks themselves haven't evolved, the cost of entry for attackers has plummeted, making enumeration free. The expensive part of an attack used to be the expert thinking, and frontier AI has made that instant, tireless and cheap. As Amy puts it, the villain is still the attacker, who now has the same capabilities defenders do.
